Oak Creek Library System
May 18 at 4:44 PM
 ·
Due to recent changes to the Collection Development Policy adopted by the Board of Trustees, staff time is being reallocated to implement these updates. As a result, many youth programs have been canceled indefinitely. Interlibrary Loan services have also been suspended, and you may experience delays in the processing and shelving of new materials. To check the current status of scheduled programs, including cancellations, please visit:
https://oakcreeklibrarysystem.libnet.info/events


Morgan Phillips for Oak Creek County Council
May 18 at 10:10 PM
 ·
County council appoints the library board. Recently, county council members appointed library board members who believe in telling librarians to follow their (the board members') personal rules about how books are shelved instead of definitions used by publishers and the American Library Association. So now, our librarians have to spend their time researching every single book in the juvenile and YA sections to decide if any should be moved into a new "teen" section the board invented. This incredibly time-intense project means that programming for young children and youth must be suspended and interlibrary loans won't run. I've asked for an investigation into the board's power to control county employees' job roles, but I am not sure it'll make a difference. Remember this at election time: county councilors and the library board members they appointed are dismantling our libraries so they can tell you what your children can read.

The library director, who fought against this censorship for years, was just fired tonight by the board. This is a sad time for our county.




After nearly two hours in private session, the Oak Creek County Library Board voted 5–2 to fire Library Director Jeanine Staples — with no public explanation. Voting against were Harry Stine and Cole Parker.
Jeanine has led our library system since 2019. She’s from Oak Creek County. She’s a career librarian with more than 20 years of experience. And just this year she received the Intellectual Freedom Award from the state’s Library Association for her work defending the freedom to read.
This decision comes right in the middle of the board’s directive to review more than 86,000 children’s and teen books — a massive undertaking that has already caused programs to be canceled and interlibrary loans to be paused so staff can focus on reviewing materials. Removing the director in the middle of this process leaves the entire library system in chaos at a time when steady leadership is needed most.
The Oak Creek County Library System should stand for access, professionalism, and transparency. A decision of this magnitude — made without explanation — leaves many of us concerned about what comes next.
If you care about our library, please stay engaged.

Carlos Rena


To the Oak Creek County Library Board and County Council,
I write today to express my deep concern and disappointment regarding the recent decisions made by several members of the Oak Creek County Library Board to restrict access to children’s books and to terminate the head librarian. These actions are misguided and threaten the open access to knowledge and learning that public libraries are meant to uphold.
Banning or restricting books based on a few quoted lines—often taken out of context from online sources—does not protect children; it only limits their ability to grow, learn, and think critically. A library should be a place where families can explore a diversity of ideas and choose what is appropriate for themselves, not where a narrow group dictates what others may read.
These new vague and subjective policies will burden library staff, invite censorship, and likely conflict with constitutional principles of free access to information. Most troubling of all, they undermine the professionalism and dedication of those who serve our community’s educational needs—such as our recently dismissed librarian, who deserved support, not punishment, for upholding the values of an open and inclusive library system.
I urge all citizens who believe in intellectual freedom and public transparency to make their voices heard. Contact the library board, the county council, and our state legislators. Ask them to reverse these harmful actions and restore integrity, fairness, and trust to our public libraries.
The freedom to read and to think for oneself is a cornerstone of this community. Let us not lose sight of that.

Katie  Uselman  Hi Katie, thank you for asking such a thoughtful question — I really appreciate your openness and willingness to learn more about what’s happening.
From my perspective, the new rules restrict access because they put added barriers between children and many books that have long been part of the library’s collection. The board’s policy allows a book to be challenged or removed if any single line is deemed objectionable, even if it’s taken out of context. Since these reviews often rely on lists from advocacy websites rather than the full text or professional librarian assessments, entire books could be pulled or hidden without a fair or balanced evaluation.
The result is that children — including your 10-year-old — might not ever see or know about books that offer perspectives their parents might have otherwise chosen for them. It shifts the decision from families to a few individuals applying subjective standards. That’s what feels concerning: it narrows the choices available to everyone rather than empowering parents to guide their own families’ reading.
I respect that people want to protect kids, and I think we share that goal. I just believe we can do that best by trusting parents and librarians to work together, while keeping the library shelves open to all kinds of voices and stories.

Task:


Could you summarize the events that have the community upset in this document?

Based on the document, the Oak Creek community is upset by a series of interconnected events centered on changes to the library's Collection Development Policy, which have led to service cuts and accusations of censorship.

Here is a summary of the key events causing the upset:

1.  **Policy Changes and Service Cuts:** The Library Board of Trustees adopted new changes to its Collection Development Policy. Implementing these updates requires a massive project to review and re-shelve over 86,000 books in the children's, juvenile, and young adult sections. This involves deciding whether to move books into a new "teen" section based on the board's subjective standards. As a result, staff time has been reallocated, leading to the indefinite cancellation of many youth programs and the suspension of interlibrary loan services.

2.  **Accusations of Ideological Censorship:** A county council candidate, Morgan Phillips, and many community members allege that the board, appointed by the council, is imposing its own ideological rules on the library. They claim the board is acting on behalf of a "vocal minority" with "extreme religious" views to dictate what children can read, bypassing professional librarian standards and the American Library Association (ALA). This is seen as an attempt to dismantle the library system to control content.

3.  **Firing of the Library Director:** In the midst of this turmoil, the Library Board voted 5-2 to fire the highly-respected Library Director, Jeanine Staples, who had served since 2019 and recently won an Intellectual Freedom Award. The firing occurred in a private session with no public explanation, leading to widespread anger and speculation that it was retaliation for her defending the freedom to read.

4.  **The Core Conflict: Censorship vs. Parental Control:** The community is deeply divided.
    *   **Critics of the board** (like Phillips, Carlos Rena, and Jenny Ellison) argue that the policy is vague and subjective, amounts to banning and censoring books (including classics and LGBTQ+ titles), and burdens staff. They see it as an attack on intellectual freedom.
    *   **Supporters of the changes** (like Lacey Robins, Teresa Wormwood, and Darla Davison) argue that moving books with mature content (sexual descriptions, nudity) to an adult or teen section is not censorship but a common-sense measure to protect minors, similar to movie ratings. They believe this empowers parents to control their children's reading choices.

5.  **Impact on Services and Community:** The immediate impact has been the loss of valued youth programs (story times, etc.) and access to materials through interlibrary loans. The community is calling for an investigation, legal challenges, and greater public engagement to reverse the board's actions and restore services.

In essence, the community is rallying against what they perceive as an undemocratic takeover of the library by a conservative-leaning board, resulting in censorship, the firing of a beloved director, and the degradation of essential public services.
